newObjects.Name: Sh 2-187
newObjects.Historical:
Discovered by Gaze and Shajn in 1952 and included in the 3rd Simeis catalogue (Simeis 113): "A small nebula, probably hydrogen." Sharpless 1-33 noted a "Small cluster in center."

GalaxyMap: This young (100-200 thousand years) star formation region is most likely ionised by a B0 class star and is surrounded by a 4600 solar mass molecular cloud. It is partially obscured by the Lynds dark nebula LDN 1317 and contains the infrared star cluster [BDS2003] 52. This nebula is prominent in infrared as can be seen in this MSX image.

Russeil lists three potential ionising stars, one with a B2.5V class.

Distance estimates
1000 pc [2001AJ....122..313J]
1440 pc +/- 260 [2007A&A...470..161R]
-----
CSOG: The emission nebula Simeis 113 is elongated and irregular and is surrounded by the dark nebula LDN 1317.
-----
2022 paper: "Fragmented atomic shell around S187 H II region and its interaction with molecular and ionized gas." (2022MNRAS.515.2445Z)
To study the atomic hydrogen gas around a H II region, high resolution H I data should be obtained and compared with kinematics, morphology and properties of other species. This paper presents such analysis for the Sh 2-187 environment. This region is well-studied from the optical to the radio wavelengths. The S187 H ii region is driven by a cluster of B0V stars historically named as S187 B or BD52. The region is fairly young with an estimated age of ~500,000 years. The distance estimate is 1.4 ± 0.26 kpc from photometry and ~0.9 kpc from Gaia DR2 data and CO line analysis of associated large-scale structures. The H II region is surrounded by a molecular and atomic gas shell. A number of young stellar objects were detected towards the shell.

The formation of IRAS 01202+6133 (M ~21 M_Sun, L ~5600 L_Sun) is argued to have been triggered by the expansion of the S187 H II region. A pre-main-sequence object S187 Ha was discovered by Zavagno et al. (1994) with a mass of 25 ± 12 M_Sun nearby to IRAS 01202+6133. A 12CO outflow is associated with S187 Ha and a molecular hydrogen outflow driven by T Tauri star S187 NIRS 1. The existence of such objects is evidence of ongoing star formation in the shell.

We report the first evidence of a clumpy HI environment in its photodissociation region. The estimated atomic mass fraction of the shell is ~260 M_Sun, the shell size is ~4 pc.  The atomic shell consists of ~100 fragments. The S187 shell has a complex kinematical structure, including the expanding quasi spherical layer, molecular envelope, an atomic sub-bubble inside the shell and two dense cores (S187 SE and S187 NE) at different stages of evolution. The atomic sub-bubble inside the shell is young, contains a Class II young stellar object.

Simeis 5: "A very small nebula to the southwest of IC 1848; apparently a purely hydrogen formation."

1991 by Pismis & Mampaso: "Infrared studies ofH ii regions: the Sharpless regions S148, 184, 198, 206 and 269"
This scarcely studied diffuse H II region, located towards the south of W5, presents an almost circular shape on the POSS red print, around the 09.5 V star LS I 59153 (Georgelin, Georgelin & Roux 1973; Lahulla 1985). S198-IRS coincides with the central star of the nebula; for a spectral type 09.5V we find D = 2.9 kpc; and no evidence of infrared excess, a barely surprising result given the advanced evolutionary stage of SI98 and the expected absence of dust grains close to the central star. S 198 is in fact one rare example of an H II region without CO emission located in an area particularly rich in molecular complexes

newObjects.Name: LBN 437
newObjects.Historical:
2025 paper by Aardra+: "Kinematic study of molecular gas in cometary globule - LBN 437" (2025MNRAS.540.2279A)
Cometary globules are isolated, relatively small molecular clouds detached from the parental molecular clouds with a cometary or a tear-shaped morphology. CGs are found in the vicinity of OB associations in the HII regions. These interstellar clouds are characterized by a compact, bright-rimmed head and a faintly luminous, diffuse tail extending away from the early-type star. CGs are a subgroup of Bok globules with a size of ~0.1 to 1.0 pc. But the origin of CGs is still uncertain, whether they are the result of pre-existing dense structures in the surrounding interstellar medium advected through the ionization front or flow instabilities.

The CG LBN 437 is located at the edge of an elongated molecular cloud complex Kh149 at the boundary of H II region, Sh 2-126. The formation of the cometary head of LBN 437 and the triggered star formation occurring in the cloud is attributed to the interaction of the cloud with the ionizing radiation from the Lac OB1 members. The brightest of the Lac OB1 members is the star 10 Lac with a spectral type O9V, located south-east of LBN 437, at an angular distance of ~1.8°. The nuclear region of LBN 437 also coincides with a reflection nebula, DG 187. LBN 437 lacks a prominent tail and resembles a comma-like morphology.

The molecular concentration named Condensation A in the cometary head is associated with an optical reflection nebula and houses a group of Ha emission line sources, namely LkHa 230, LkHa 231, LkHa 232 and LkHa 233. The formation of these young stars might be triggered by radiation-driven implosion, in which UV radiation from a luminous star such as 10 Lac causes the evaporation and compression of the molecular cloud.
Summary: The estimated mass infall rate indicates a collapse phase, with accretion rates high enough to facilitate the formation of highmass stars. In conjunction with the presence of LkHa sources, this implies that LBN 437 might be undergoing clustered star formation consistent with models of competitive accretion.

historicalUpdates.Name: NGC 2163
historicalUpdates.Historical:
Édouard Stephan discovered NGC 2163 = St. 9-6 on 31 Jan 1873.  He made a second observation on 29 Dec 1877 and reduced the position again a week later (6 Jan 1878).  His description reads, "extremely faint, elongated, diffuse, *11 attached south."

In compiling the NGC, Dreyer accidentally copied the declination of NGC 1741 (Stephan's previous entry in list 9, #5).  Dreyer later caught and corrected his error in the IC 2 Notes/Corrections section (Dreyer added the comment "my mistake").  The correction was missed by most later cataloguers, although Esmiol's 1916 re-reduction of Stephan's positions gives the accurate position.

In 1922, Edwin Hubble reported it as a new "bright, uncatalogued nebula similar to NGC 2245" (#15 in a list of "Diffuse Nebulae with continuous spectra") and commented "It is surprising to find that so bright an object has been overlooked by observers."  Based on Hubble's listing, Sven Cederblad catalogued it as an "anonymous" nebula (#62) in his 1946 catalog of "Bright Diffuse Galactic Nebulae", with credit to Hubble.  I also uncovered that E.E. Barnard independently discovered NGC 2163 on 2 Sep 1888. On his first observation he mistook it for Faye's Comet, which he was searching for.  Barnard never published his rediscovery.

Modern sources generally identify NGC 2163 as Cederblad 62.  The RNGC labels NGC 2163 as nonexistent and furthermore reverses the sign of the declination.  In addition, a poor RA was given for Ced 62 in Sky Catalogue 2000 and it was misplotted on the Uranometria 2000 (first edition) too far east, though the position was corrected in the second edition.  The Millenium Star Atlas labels this object Ced 62, also at the wrong position.

historicalUpdates.Name: NGC 2311
historicalUpdates.Historical:
According to Wolfgang Steinicke, Caroline Herschel discovered NGC 2311 = H. VIII-60 = h418 on 4 Mar 1783, probably with a small refractor.  She logged, "in the neighborhood of the 17 Monoceros, a Nebula, very obscure.  Messier has it not."  She entered this object as #4 in her discovery log and William checked it immediately with his 6.2" reflector.  NGC 2311 is situated 1.3° WSW of the star (modern identification 19 Mon), so this identification seems likely.

William Herschel independently discovered NGC 2311 on 26 Nov 1786 (sweep 639) and described "a cluster of pL scattered stars, not very rich.  The place taken is the most compressed part, but not the middle.  May be a projecting point of the milky way."  His position was just northeast of center of this cluster.  William was credited with the discovery in the NGC as he mistakenly identified NGC 2349 (H. VII 27) as Caroline's discovery.

historicalUpdates.Name: IC 2177
historicalUpdates.Historical:
Isaac Roberts discovered IC 2177 photographically in 1898 surrounding mag 7.3 BD -10°1848.  His position (for the mag 7 star) and dimensions of 13' corresponds with the position of vdB 93 = Gum 1 = Sh 2-292, *not* the 2° N-S strip of nebulosity (Seagull Nebula) that is commonly identified as IC 2177 in modern catalogues.

Max Wolf discovered the often-photographed Seagull Nebula (Gum 2 = Sh 2-296) in 1905.  In 1906 he wrote, "During the past year I found on two plates taken with small lenses a wonderfully beautiful and bright, extended nebulous patch which, as far as I can determine, has until now remained unknown. It lies for the most part in Canis Major; its northern portions extend into Monoceros. The nebula was photographed several times with smaller instruments and then also with the Bruce telescope. It covers many square degrees and encloses the following four Durchmusterung stars: BD -11°1747, -10°1848, -12°1771, and -11°1790." He adds "“The associated cavities adjoin these nebulous masses to the west," suggesting an early reference to his "Cave Nebulae".  Wolf was quickly notified by Robert's widow of the prior discovery of the northern nebula surrounding BD -10°1848, and Wolf printed a correction noting "It therefore follows that Dr. Roberts is to be credited with the discovery of this nebula, although he did not know its extensive eastern and southern portions, particularly the almost brightest part around the star -12°1771."

Dreyer only credited Roberts with the discovery of IC 2177 and his description is basically from Roberts, but his position is 18' SE of BD -10°1848.  Corwin states that he may have been influenced somewhat by Wolf's description of the larger nebula (Stephen O'Meara makes a similar argument), but this is never mentioned so it is speculative.  A strict interpretation of the IC 1 is that IC 2177 refers just to Gum 1.

The Seagull Nebula was also found on a photograph taken on 1 Apr 1911 by Harry Wood at the Transvaal (Union) Observatory with the 10-inch Franklin-Adams camera.  Wood described a "large faint straggling region, about 2 1/2° long."  He added "BD -10° 1848 is involved in a bright patch of nebulosity, in which there are two large holes on the S side of the star."  It was first catalogued in 1950 in [Str50] 18 and  Gum 1 in 1955.  But Hans Vehrenberg's Atlas of Deep-Sky Splendours described IC 2177 as an H II region more than 3° in extent and the 1985 Sky Catalogue 2000.0 also gave the dimensions of IC 2177 as 120'x40'.

historicalUpdates.Name: NGC 2349
historicalUpdates.Historical:
William Herschel discovered NGC 2349 = H. VII-27 = h436 on 24 Feb 1786 (sweep 529).  He recorded, "An irregular cluster of extremely small stars, considerably compressed, 9 or 10' long, 4 or 5' broad with an extending branch towards sp."  Close to his position (Auwers' reduction) is the group of stars described in my observation.  John Herschel logged this object on 8 Jan 1831 (sweep 318) as a "a poor straggling cl, place of a double star", but his position is 1 min of RA too far west and corresponds with a mag 10/11.5 at 30" separation that is not involved in any clustering.  Unfortunately JH used his own position in the GC and it was repeated by Dreyer in the NGC.

William added the comment to VII 27 (second catalogue) "Caroline Herschel discovery 1783".  But according to Wolfgang Steinicke, she never observed this object and William must be referring to NGC 2311 instead, which she discovered on 4 Mar 1783.

Based on Heidelberg plates, Karl Reinmuth noted "many st in a dense region, very little clustering."  RNGC classifies the number nonexistent (Type 7).  See Harold Corwin's identification notes.

His position is 1.5 minutes of time to the west of the galaxy (~8 arcminutes) and a mag 8 star is 5' north, so the identification is certain.

historicalUpdates.Name: IC 5067
historicalUpdates.Historical: Rev. Thomas Espin discovered IC 5067 visually, along with IC 5068 and 5070, on 7 Sep 1899 with his 17.25-inch Calver reflector. He simply noted it was "faint".  There is nothing at his position, about 37' west of the neck of the Pelican Nebula (IC 5070).  Harold Corwin suggests that if Espin's declination was off by 1.4°, then IC 5067 corresponds with IC 5068B, described here.  Espin's positions for IC 5068 and 5070 are good, so otherwise IC 5067 is lost without additional information, but Corwin notes that IC 5068B is the brightest nebula in the region that he might have picked up. Another option is that Espin picked up the neck of the Pelican Nebula and made an error in RA.

The mag 13.5-14 globular was clearly nonstellar, though very small, ~8" diameter with a bright, quasi-stellar center and fainter halo.  With direct vision the brighter center dominates and the halo fades.  The globular forms the east vertex of a tiny equilateral triangle with two mag 14.5/15 stars 8" NW and SW.

18" (9/20/03): at 215x appears as a slightly out of focus "star" forming a tight triple with two faint stars.  At 323x it resolves into a very small, 14th magnitude knot, ~10" diameter, forming a tight triangle with two mag 14/15 stars at the SW and NW edges, less than 10" from the center.  M31-G1 and its two stellar companions form a near equilateral triangle with two mag 12/13 stars ~2' NNE and NE.

17.5" (8/22/98 and 9/28/02): easily picked up sweeping at 220x because on first glance it appears to be a close but cleanly resolved mag 14 triple star!  On closer viewing, the central "star" is soft or slightly nebulous and surrounded by a very faint and small halo ~10" diameter.  The foreground mag 14.5-15 companion stars are situated at the NW and SW edges of the halo just 8" and 9" from the center of the globular, respectively.  UGC 330 lies 11' ESE and M31-G2, another faint M31 globular, lies 10' SE.

17.5" (10/21/95): this is the brightest globular cluster within M31 and appears as a fuzzy mag 14 object about 10" diameter with a bright quasi-stellar nucleus.  The view is confused by a mag 14.5-15 star at the SW end and a fainter more difficult star at the NW edge of the halo.  G1 is situated 2.5° SW of the center of M31!

8" (8/18/01): seen in Matt Marcus' C8, though it was difficult to make out in the field at high power.  I doubt the attached stars were resolved.

visualUpdates.Name: M31-G002
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (10/5/26): at 327x; this M31 globular appeared as a faint, soft, non-stellar glow ~3" in diameter. Situated 2' SW of UGC 330 and 0.8' SSW of a mag 14.5 star.  G1 lies 10' WNW.

18" (12/8/07): at 300x as a very faint mag 15.5-15.8 "star (perhaps slightly easier than listed V mag of 15.8).  Located just 2' SW of UGC 330 and 10' ESE of M31-G1.

17.5" (9/28/02): at 324x, this M31 globular appears as a mag 15.5 "star" (V = 15.8) just 51" SSW of a mag 14 star and 2' SW of UGC 330!  M31-G1, the brightest globular in M31, lies 10' WNW.

visualUpdates.Name: UGC 330
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (10/5/26): at 327x; fairly faint, very elongated 3:1 NW-SE, ~0.6'x0.2', small bright core.  A mag 14.5 star is 1.4' SW and the faint M31 globular cluster G2 is 2' SW.

18" (12/8/07): faint, small, elongated 2:1 NW-SE, ~30"x15", broad weak concentration to a rounder 15" core with fainter extensions.  This galaxy is located 11' WSW of the bright M31 globular G1 and is good reference point for the faint gc G2, situated just 2' SW.

17.5" (9/28/02): very faint, small, elongated 2:1 NW-SE, 0.5'x0.2', very small brighter core.  A mag 14 star lies 1.3' SW and M31-G2 is 2' SW!  Located in the field of M31-G1 11' WNW.

17.5" (10/17/98): very faint, small, slightly elongated NW-SE, weak concentration (I probably only viewed the core).  A couple of mag 14.5 stars are within 1.5' including one 1.3' SW and a star a similar distance to the north.  Located 4' SSW of mag 8.8 SAO 53990 and 11' ESE of M31-G1, the brightest globular in M31!

visualUpdates.Name: LEDA 2152244
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (10/5/26): at 327x; this galaxy (originally classified as a M31 globular) appeared as a faint to very faint non-stellar glow, just 6" or so in diameter. Situated 2.3' S of a mag 10.8 star, which is an unequal 15" pair.

18" (12/8/07): appears as a mag 15.6 "star" to the east of G1 and G2 and between the very faint galaxies UGC 338 and UGC 344.  There are a couple of brighter stars nearby including a mag 10.5 star 2.2' N that makes pinpointing the position easy.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 225
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (1/4/14): bright, large, scattered group of ~50 stars in 10' group.  Includes 15-18 brighter stars that stand out (mag 9.5-11).  A ragged N-S string of stars defines the eastern border of the cluster.  There are no rich subgroups and there's a lack of faint stars.

A detached group of stars is off the N side, but these stars do not appear to be part of the cluster.  vdB 4, a very faint reflection nebula, is involved with these stars though it was not noticed.

17.5" (11/2/91): about two dozen stars at 100x in a 12' diameter.  Bright but scattered.  Outline forms an isosceles triangle with the vertex at west edge and the long base on the east side.  Most stars are mag 10-11 and evenly spaced.  The cluster appears completely resolved.  Only one fairly close double star in group.  Just ENE of the main group is a line of five mag 9 stars oriented N-S.

8": two dozen stars in a cluster, fairly bright but scattered, no dense spots.

15x50mm (10/14/23): large, 12'-15' diameter, partially resolved with a half-dozen mag 9.5-10.5 stars

visualUpdates.Name: M31-G318
visualUpdates.Visual Description: 24" (10/5/26): at 375x; very faint GC in M31, appears non-stellar ~3"-4" diameter.  Forms the northern vertex of a small isosceles triangle with a mag 10.3 star 1.5' SW and an 11.4 mag star 1.7' SE.

visualUpdates.Name: UGC 529
visualUpdates.Visual Description: 24" (10/6/26): at 375x; moderately bright, very elongated at least 3:1 E-W, ~45"x15", strong concentration with a bright bulge.  A 10" pair of mag 11.5 stars is 2.7' WSW.

visualUpdates.Name: UGC 540
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (10/6/26): at 375x; fairly faint (relatively bright UGC), elongated NW-SE, ~0.6'x0.4', brighter core. The galaxy appeared clumpy with a hint of spiral structure (curved brightening in the halo). A mag 14.8 star is just off the NE edge and a mag 15.5 star is 50" SW of center.  The galaxy is located 2.7' SSE of a mag 8.8 star. 

24" (11/24/14): at 375x; fairly faint, fairly small, roughly 3:2 NW-SE, but seems to change orientation slightly with averted vision, fairly even surface brightness, ~27"x18".  Located 2.7' SSE of mag 8.8 SAO 74336 and 9' WSW of mag 7.3 HD 5138.  Picked up while observing edge-on UGC 542 located 15' NNE.

visualUpdates.Name: UGC 567
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (10/6/26): at 327x; fairly faint, elongated SW-NE, a small bright core dominates over the faint extensions. A mag 14.9 star is 0.6' N.  Forms a pair with UGC 566 just 1.2' S.

17.5" (11/25/87): faint, very small, round, small bright core.  A mag 14 star is 1' NNW.  Located 13' NNE of NGC 296.  Brightest of three with UGC 566 1' S (not seen) and (R)NGC 296 = UGC 565 3' S (not seen).

visualUpdates.Name: UGC 2855
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (1/13/26): at 263x; large oval glow WNW-ESE, low surface brightness, ~2.5'x 1.2'. An 11th mag star is superimposed on the northern edge and detracts from viewing. The portion of the galaxy west of the star is more evident. Situated 6' SE of mag 8.3 HD 23102.  UGC 2866 is 10' ESE.

In 1954, Gaze and Shajn discovered this galaxy during a survey of emission nebulae and catalogued it as Simeis 284.

visualUpdates.Name: Sh 2-232
visualUpdates.Visual Description: 14.5" (1/7/24): NVD at 24x; Sh 2-232 is by far the largest of four HII regions in a group with Sh 2-231, 2-233 and 2-235.  Overall, Sh 2-232 has a moderate and fairly low surface brightness over its 35' diameter. Nevertheless,this is a fascinating object with a wreath-like appearance and a fairly bright, long filament or band stretching E to W for 30' on the south side and passing 8' S of the mag 8.1 ionizing star HD 37737. The band is slightly brighter at the west end where there is a perpendicular (N-S) brightening.  The northern side has a weak filamentary appearance with darker areas. The high-surface-brightness HII region Sh 2-235 is 27' SW of HD 37737.

visualUpdates.Name: Sh 2-249
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (1/7/24): NVD at 24x;  Courtès 138 = Sh 2-249 is a huge and interesting HII region about 1° ENE of the IC 443 supernova remnant. Previously I had noticed a long, thin filament extending east from IC 443 (part of Simeis 41). Continuing just another 1/2° further E, I found a fairly bright and very large field of nebulosity elongated N-S (Simeis 42), ~50'x30'. The outline appeared highly irregular with interior dark lanes.

On the west side is a mag 8.3 star HD 44252.  A thin, irregular dust lane loops south and east from this star and then heads north for ~10', where it nearly reaches a 10th mag star that is surrounded by darker circular region. More prominently, a high contrast, very long and broad dust lane runs N-S near the east edge for roughly 25', with the southern end close to 2.9-magnitude Mu Gem.  Very diffuse nebulosity is on the east side of the lane. The north end of the Sh 2-249 complex was patchy with brighter and darker areas, but no distinct dust lanes.

visualUpdates.Name: IC 4593
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (9/7/26): bright, very small, bluish, but clearly non-stellar at 158x. At 395x, appeared slightly elongated ~N-S and the bright central star was visible in moments of good seeing.  UGC 10238 lies 24' NW.

24" (6/30/22): at 109x; shows a distinct "blinking" effect.  Staring directly emphasizes the bright blue central star, but with averted a small halo is prominent.  Increasing to 457x, a prominent central star is encased in a very well defined, slightly elongated halo ~4:3 in a N-S orientation.

14.5" (7/11/21): identified very easily at 140x as a fairly bright, fuzzy blue "star".  Good, but not excellent, contrast gain with an OIII filter. At 226x, a small 10" disc surrounds a clearly seen central star in the high surface brightness glow. Increasing to 352x, the central star was much more prominent and the halo was slightly elongated NNW-SSE and seemed irregular.  A mag 9.4 star is 5' NW and the double star STF 2016 is 11' SE.  The planetary is along the line connecting these objects.

18" (7/20/06): at 160x the 10.5-mag central star is encased by a small, oval halo, elongated NNW-SSE, ~10"x7".  The planetary has the characteristic blue glow seen in this class of objects.  Good response to OIII blinking at this power.  The central star is more prominent at 225x and 325x but there were no additional details visible in fairly poor seeing.

17.5" (5/10/86): at 286x a bright 11th magnitude central star is visible surrounded by a small, slightly elongated halo, bluish color.  Located 11' NW of double star STF 2016 = 8.5/9.6 at 7".

8" (6/30/22): at 109x, IC 4593 was easily identified as a blue 11th mag fuzzy star situated 5' SE of a brighter mag 9.4 star.  Adding a NPB filter provides an excellent contrast gain and the planetary appears to outshine the star.

8" (6/81): stellar at 100x but a slightly elongated disc is easy to view at 220x-350x.  Located 12' NW of a mag 9 star.

visualUpdates.Name: Abell 39
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (7/7/13): easily visible unfiltered at 200x as a large, round, low surface brightness disc.  The mag 15-15.5 central star was visible at this power or higher (used 282x) as well as a superimposed mag 15.5-16 on the south side [50" SSW of the central star].  Best view was at 125x using a UHC filter.  With this combination, this Abell planetary was clearly annular with a narrow, unevenly lit rim.  A small brighter segment is at the S end and the rim is brighter in a thin strip along the entire E side.

24" (7/19/12): viewed at 200x with an NPB filter.  The rim of this large planetary is slightly brighter in an unevenly lit thin ring.  The brightest arc is along the E and SE rim (roughly a 70°-80° arc).  A narrow strip of the rim is also enhanced along the W and SW side (roughly an 80°-90° arc), mostly S of a mag 14 star just off the W side of the planetary (1.8' W of center).  The rim is perhaps weakest along the NW edge.  A faint galaxy, MCG +05-39-003, lies 12' ENE.

18" (7/14/07): Abell 39 was easily picked up at 115x with an OIII filter. It appeared as a weakly annular, sharply defined disc, nearly 3' in diameter.  The rim appeared unevenly lit with a couple of slightly brighter arc segments when I let the planetary drift through the field.  Abell 39 was faintly visible unfiltered, though there was a crisper view with a narrowband filter.

18" (7/20/06): visible unfiltered at 115x as a large, low surface brightness, roundish glow 2'-3' in diameter.  Adding an OIII filter gave more definition and structure though the contrast gain was not dramatic.  The thick rim is slightly brighter, though not uniform around, giving a weak annular appearance with an ill-defined, slightly darker center.

18" (7/18/04): viewed at 115x (20 Nagler) and an OIII filter.  Appeared as a faint, fairly large, well-defined disc.  With averted vision and concentration the rim is slightly brighter (possibly in arcs along the west and east sides), giving a weakly annular appearance.  Very faintly visible unfiltered at 115x, though the shape is more formless without a crisp boundary, but it was now noticeable that the planetary is set in a rich star field.

18" (6/20/04): swept up immediately at 115x using an OIII filter.  Visible continuously as a crisp-edged disc, round, ~2.5' in diameter.  Although there was no annularity there were subtle irregularities in the surface brightness.  Barely visible unfiltered, though the glow seemed to merge into the background sky without a distinct edge.  Also, excellent view at 73x and OIII filter as the planetary was easily viewed continuously with direct vision.

17.5" (8/21/98): picked up at 100x with an OIII filter.  Once identified, it was visible continuously with direct vision as a round, sharp-edged disc at least 2.5' in diameter.  It appeared slightly brighter along the following edge.  The planetary was even faintly visible unfiltered at 100x, though not as sharp-edged or well-defined and several faint stars were superimposed.

13.1" (6/18/85): faint, fairly large, round.  This planetary can just be held steadily with averted vision using an OIII filter which provided a superior view to the Daystar 300.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 6240
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
48" (4/6/13 and 5/21/23): NGC 6240, a highly disrupted merger, appeared fairly bright, moderately large, elongated 3:2 SSW-NNE, ~1.2'x0.8', irregular shape!  A prominent, thin extension or spike extends 4:1 or 5:1 to the NNE from the central region.  This wing is sharply defined and narrow.  A short, bright, broader extension juts out to the SSW, in the opposite direction of the NNE wing.  Finally, a faint short wing (~15"x5") extends S from the central region on the E side (on the DSS, this branch curves at the south end).  A mag 13.5 star is 30" E, a mag 15.5-16 star is 0.8' SSE and a 12" pair of mag 13.5/15 stars lies 1.5' S.

LEDA 214549, located 4' NNE, was easily seen as a thin edge-on SW-NE, ~0.7'x0.1', with a slightly brighter core.

24" (7/22/14): the Rumpled Starfish appeared fairly faint to moderately bright, moderately large, irregular but roughly elongated 3:2 SSW-NNE, ~60"x40", though it increased in size with averted vision.  The surface brightness is irregular, with a mottled texture.  The brightest portion had an offset nucleus or knot on the east side.  On the NE side, a faint narrow wing extended to the N.  A very short extension was also glimpsed on the SE side.  A mag 13.5 star is 0.6' NE and a mag 15.7 star is 50" SSE of center.

24" (8/15/12): this irregular galaxy appeared fairly faint, moderately large, elongated 2:1 SSW-NNE, ~1.0'x0.5', broad concentration with a slightly brighter core.  The shape is unusual as the NNE end is narrow, like an edge-on, while the SSW end appears wider. With careful viewing, a very faint extension branches south from the central region, creating a forked appearance with the brighter portion trending SSW.  A mag 13.5 star is 0.6' NE and a mag 15.5 star is 0.8' SE of center.

18" (7/22/03): fairly faint, fairly small, elongated 2:1 SSW-NNE, 0.8'x0.4', weak concentration, appears slightly brighter along the major axis.  With extended viewing, there is an impression of an irregular shape with a very faint extension off the main bar near the center.

17.5" (6/8/91): fairly faint, small, elongated 2:1 SW-NE, even surface brightness.  A mag 13 star is at the NE edge 0.6' from center.

visualUpdates.Name: Haute-Provence 1
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (7/4/24): Night-vision at 34x (unfiltered); HP 1 is a fairly prominent small glow.  Just increasing to 56x (41mm Panoptic), the view was significantly improved. The nucleus was obvious as a stellar or quasi-stellar knot at the center and at least a half-dozen stars were resolved over the glow of the halo.

24" (7/4/24): at 327x; HP 1 is an easy soft glow, ~1.5' diameter with a small brighter nucleus. The globular is cradled around the north side by an equally spaced trio of mag 12.5-13 stars with a brighter mag 10.7 star 2.5' NE.  The diameter of the halo is roughly the distance between the outer stars in the trio [measured later at 1.5'].  Only a few stars were detected within the disk.  HP 1 is projected at only 3.3° from the Galactic center

24" (7/29/16): HP 1 was obvious in the field at 200x, just south of a shallow arc of three mag 12.5-13 stars, 1.5'-2' diameter, roundish, small slightly brighter nucleus.  The view was improved at 375x.  The core region stood out better and 1 or 2 stars were resolved at the edge of the nucleus.  Also 1 or 2 stars were resolved around the edges of the halo and a couple more sparkles within the halo.

17.5" (6/3/00): extremely faint, small roundish glow visible with averted vision only, 1.0'-1.5' in diameter.  Situated just south of a shallow arc of three mag 13 stars.  A mag 10.7 star lies 2.5' NE.  The highly reddened globular is set against an unresolved Milky Way background and is just brighter than the background glow.  Located 49' ESE of 4.3-magnitude 45 Ophiuchi.

visualUpdates.Name: M 1-88
visualUpdates.Visual Description: 17.5" (7/18/01): picked up at 64x using a UHC filter as a moderately bright, 3'x2.5' glow, slightly elongated N-S.  The eastern side has a sharper, linear border.  Also viewed at 220x unfiltered and a group of a half dozen mag 12-13 stars extended N-S in a string are superimposed near the eastern boundary.  This obscure, but relatively easy nebula is located 30' N of NGC 6604 and Sh 2-54 (a large, faint HII region encasing the cluster).

visualUpdates.Name: M 3-34
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (9/15/26): I first identified M 3-34 at just 66x by blinking the fairly rich star field with an OIII filter. At 158x, it appeared as a soft blue star with an excellent contrast gain using a NPB filter. The PN is aligned with a mag 12.6 star 3' SW and a 10th mag star 6' SW.

Increasing to 395x displayed an obvious bluish disc perhaps 5"-8" diameter. Occasionally, I seemed to get a flash of a central star, though it is listed at only 16th magnitude.  At 660x, the disc was round with a pale blue color and fuzzy edges.

17.5" (8/1/86): at 220x with OIII filter a small disc less than 10" diameter is visible.  Bright and pretty view at 286x unfiltered.

visualUpdates.Name: Czernik 41
visualUpdates.Visual Description: 14.5" (9/5/26): at 226x; fairly distinctive 8' group with three bright mag 9.6 (HD 339022), 9.9 (HD 339023), and 10.0 (HD 339021) stars. Also includes a quadrilateral of mag 10-12 stars on the W side, along with two 14th mag stars.  A 10" pair of mag 13.5/14.2 stars is on the E side.  About a dozen stars in total were identified.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 6830
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (9/7/26): over 50 stars resolved at 226x in the central region. Many of the stars are aligned in chains, including two oriented WSW-ENE and NNW-SSE that intersect near the center at right angles. The NNW includes a group of half-dozen stars. The two brightest stars are mag 10.0 and 10.8, both along these intersecting arms. 

17.5" (8/8/91): 30-35 stars in the central 5' diameter.  Most stars are mag 11-12 and arranged in two rows forming a rough "X" shape.  The richest group is at the NW corner and a very faint group is off the SW corner.  The brightest star is just SW of the intersection point of the "X".  Located 30' N of 4.9-magnitude 12 Vulpeculae.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 6834
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (9/7/26): NGC 6834 is an attractive cluster at 132x with the brighter stars aligned WSW-ENE and passing just north of the center of the cluster. At 226x, this cluster is rich and contains 50-60 stars in a 6' circle.  Quite a number of fainter stars huddle around the brightest mag 9.8 star (triple WSI 13). A faint arc of stars is at the S edge of the cluster.

17.5" (8/7/91): 40 visible stars in a 8' diameter.  A mag 10 star is in the middle of a line of seven mag 13 stars oriented SW-NE and also at the center of four mag 11/12 stars on a line oriented E-W.  Sprays of stars emanate from the bright star to the SW and SE.  A small clump of five stars lies 4' S of the mag 10 star.  Planetary nebula NGC 6842 lies 38' ESE.

visualUpdates.Name: Harvard 20
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (9/5/26): up to 50 stars are resolved at 226x in a 8'x4' group, elongated roughly WNW-ESE.  The two brightest stars are mag 8.9 HD 350801 (N of center) and mag 9.2 HD 350800 on the W end. A 14" matched pair is at the E end, and an unequal 11" pair is just over 1' to its W. In total, there are 8 or 9 brighter stars and the cluster is set in a rich star field. The cluster is located 24' SE of mag 6.3 9 Sge and 28' SSW of M71.

17.5" (7/28/92): about three dozen stars in a 6'x3' field, elongated ~E-W.  Two bright mag 9 stars are off the west side but the cluster is dominated by 20 mag 12/13 stars.  Also includes a scattering of faint mag 14-15 stars.  A pretty evenly matched mag 12.5/12.5 double star is at the E end and an uneven mag 12/14 double star is to the west of the well matched double.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 6837
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (9/5/26): at 226x; about 15 stars within 5' are resolved in this asterism. A string of three mag 12-13 stars (oriented NW-SE) is at the S end.  A mag 11.8 star is close to the center of the group, and a clump of 4-5 stars over haze is N of center.

17.5" (6/24/95): this asterism only stands out reasonably well at 100x.  Consists of roughly 15 mag 12-14 stars in a 4' group elongated E-W.  There is a small rich subgroup bulging out on the north side in a semi-circular arrangement (better resolved at 225x).  Listed as nonexistent in RNGC.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 6846
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (9/5/26): at 226x; appears as a small, faint mottled patch about 1' diameter, but there was no clear resolution. About 2.5' NW is a small group of 8 stars with the brightest mag 11.8 star at the NE end. This group was more eye-catching than the glowing patch.

17.5" (9/7/91): at 225x appears as a small, faint clump of stars over unresolved haze.  Elongated about 3:2 E-W with dimensions 1.5'x1.0'.  A mag 13.5 star is off the NW edge, a mag 14 star is at the W edge and three additional mag 14 stars in a clump are just visible over of the haze, although clean resolution is difficult.

K 4-41, an extremely faint stellar planetary is situated just 2' NE!  It wasn't visible without a filter, even using the ESO-Strausberg finder chart.  But adding an OIII filter, I was able to glimpse it several times about 15" S of a mag 14 star. It appeared stellar and roughly mag 16.0-16.5V.

visualUpdates.Name: Berkeley 49
visualUpdates.Visual Description: 14.5" (9/5/26): at 226x; Berkeley 49 appeared as a small glowing patch, perhaps 2' across. Only a couple of very faint stars were resolved, and a mag 14.7 star at the W edge. Located 7.5' E of mag 8.6 HD 226922.

visualUpdates.Name: Espin 202
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (9/5/26): excellent multiple star or compact cluster at 226x with 4 main components. The brightest mag 9.2 component is at the NW end.  The star at the NE side is a close, unbalanced pair making 5 stars. Two fainter stars extended SW and a couple more are separated about 1' ESE. So, there are at least 7 in the main knot plus two detached at the E edge.

18" (10/8/05): striking knot of stars including mag 9.2 HD 227247 at the NW side.  Three brighter stars to the east form a pretty quadruple though the NE star has a fainter companion.  The four stars following the mag 9 star form a trapezoid with one short base (the double).  To the SW are a string of 3 stars (one very close to the lucida), making a total of 8 stars in the knot.

17.5" (7/18/01): pretty quadruple kite-shape group with brightest star at the NW corner (SAO 69299).  The NE star also has a close, faint companion at 220x and heading SW from the bright star is a close perfectly collinear string of three mag 13.5-14 stars.  Appears almost like a tiny open cluster.  Mentioned in Aug 1998 Sky & Tel and described as a "baseball diamond".  Appears to be involved with the HII region Sh 2-101.

visualUpdates.Name: Do 36
visualUpdates.Visual Description: 14.5" (9/5/26): at 176x; about 60 scattered stars resolved in a 12' circle. This is a fairly nice group with most of the stars roughly forming a squashed oval about 9' by 5'.  The brightest star in this part is mag 9.4. At the northern end is another mag 9.4 star that forms a wide pair (~30") and a few others nearby.  About 4' to its east is another mag 9.5 (V420 Cyg) and a wide pair is just to its W.  A faint E-W chain of stars is on the NW side of the group.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 6858
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (9/7/26): at 226x, very elongated group oriented SW-NE (wider at the SW end and tapering at the NE end). A total of 30-32 stars were resolved just W of mag 9.2 HD 356626. Includes a linear string of 4 stars NW-SE on the S side that includes an 11th mag star.  The string "points" to a very small clump of faint stars to its NW. Near the center is HJ 1466, a 10" pair of mag 12.6/12.8 stars. Another short string of 3 stars SW-NE is at the NE end of the cluster.  

17.5" (9/23/95): this is an elongated group of 35 stars in a 10'x4' group oriented N-S which precedes a mag 9 star at 20 03 16 +11 16.4 (2000).  Fairly uniform in brightness and distribution with no dense spots but includes a couple of nice doubles.  Most stars are mag 12-13 with a scattering of fainter stars.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 6866
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (9/7/26): excellent, rich cluster at 132x and 226x, with ~50 stars in the central part including several pairs. Many of the stars are in generally E-W stream. ES 85, a triple star just N of center, consists of a mag 10.5 primary and two mag 12.5/13.1 companions at 11".  A faint mag 14.5 star is 0.6' E. Another trio of stars (not in ADS) is just 1' SE.  Another small clump of 3-4 stars is 3' SE of ES 85.

17.5" (9/7/91): about 100 stars in a 20'x10' region are visible at 100x.  Appears rich and very appealing.  The main string is very elongated roughly E-W and contains a brighter intersecting subgroup 8'x2' NW-SE of about 45 stars with a close triple star (ES 85) on the NW end consisting of a mag 10.5 primary (itself a 2.2" pair) and two faint mag 12.5 and 13.1 companions, both at 11".  Two mag 11/11.5 stars are at the SE end of this string.  The western end of the main string curves north into a nice semi-circle.

visualUpdates.Name: Berkeley 84
visualUpdates.Visual Description: 14.5" (9/5/26): at 226x; fairly small glowing patch with 6 or 7 faint stars resolved. A mag 10.6 star (HD 227483) is just off the W edge.

visualUpdates.Name: IC 4954
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (9/5/26): at 176x, very small, round glow surrounding a star at the N end of the stellar group Roslund 4. A group of at least 3 stars 1.5' S also appears to be faintly glowing. A parallel line of 3 stars another 1' S does not appear nebulous.

17.5" (9/26/92): this moderately bright reflection nebulosity forms a fairly striking compact pair with IC 4955 4' SE.  Very small, round, 15"-20" diameter.  Appears to surround a mag 13 star.  A distinctive group of five stars (part of Roslund 4) just south are arranged in two parallel rows of three stars and two stars.  No contrast gain with OIII or Deep Sky filter.

visualUpdates.Name: IC 4955
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (9/5/26): at 176x; fairly prominent, irregular reflection glow surrounding a 12th mag star, along with three or four fainter stars. IC 4954 is 4' NW. Both are within the cluster Roslund 4, which has a total of 18-20 stars.

17.5" (9/26/92): at 140x appears as the larger and slightly brighter of a pair of reflection nebulae with IC 4954 4' NW.  Surrounds a mag 12 star, elongated 2:1 SW-NE, 1' diameter.  A line of three mag 13.5 stars is close southeast.  No contrast enhancement with OIII or Deep Sky filter.

visualUpdates.Name: Roslund 4
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (9/5/26): at 226x; the cluster consists of two main parts, each accompanied by a reflection nebula (IC 4954 and IC 4955).  The NW group includes a close double (~7" separation) and a third star about 20" NW. Just over 1' N is a small reflection glow surrounding a singe star (IC 4954).  Just over 1' S of the triple star is a line of three mag 11.5-12.5 stars oriented NW-SE.

The SE group consists of a mag 11-12 star surrounded by a relatively bright glow (IC 4955), along with 3-4 fainter stars.  In total the cluster has a total of 18-20 stars in a 6' circle.

17.5" (9/26/92): small group of stars that illuminate the reflection nebulae IC 4954 and 4955.  Includes a group of 5 stars aligned in two parallel rows of two and three stars along with the illuminating stars of the reflection nebulae.

visualUpdates.Name: DoDz 10
visualUpdates.Visual Description: 14.5" (9/5/26): at 176x; this is a fairly large, scattered, and very elongated group of stars oriented N-S for ~18'. Mag 7.2 HD 190812 lies just off the N end. A 5' subgroup is at the S end with a triple star in its center. Towards the middle of DoDz 10 is a mag 9.3 star with a ~12" pair 1.3' to its SE. Another subgroup is at the NE end and it includes two mag 10.1 and 10.4 stars.  Roughly 70 stars were counted within these two subgroups and the main N-S stream of stars.

visualUpdates.Name: IC 1318(b)
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (8/20/25): NVD at 34x; IC 1318(b) — called IC 1318a by Gaze/Shajn and Cederblad — which connects to DWB 59 on the SW end, is an extremely large, gorgeous region of nebulosity (high surface brightness, brightness variations, and very irregular shape) is located 2° NW of Gamma Cyg.  This section of the Gamma Cyg complex extends 1.0° from SW-NE with the more narrow SW end angled SSW and faintly connected to DWB 59.  The large, broader central region is elongated from WSW to ENE and contains two mag 7.9 and 9.5 stars with a mag 9.1 just off the W side.

From the central region, slightly fainter nebulosity spreads north for nearly 15' and brightens a little at the N end.  A thinner, fainter arm extends ~15' further ENE from the central region, and a faint detached piece of nebulosity, ~6'x3', is off the S side of this arm.  In general, all of the nebulosity in the entire region (IC 1318(b) and LBN 239) visible on the DSS could be seen within two eyepiece fields.

14.5" (10/5/23, Albany): NVD at 24x.  IC 1318(b) is a very impressive section of the Gamma Cyg nebula and was strikingly prominent, even in the very bright skies at home. The entire outline shown on MegaStar was easily visible, stretching 1° from SW to NE and nearly filling the low power field.  The main body is quite elongated and includes a thin fainter "finger" of nebulosity at the east end. A small 3'x2' patch off its south side is cut off by a dark lane.  A bulbous extension, ~10' diameter, is on the north side.  The west side bends towards the south and thins at the SW end, nearly connecting with DWB 59, a fainter region of nebulosity further SW.

18" (8/11/07): This large section is situated roughly two degrees NW of Gamma Cyg (Sadr) and possibly the brightest region of the complex.  It was easily picked up in my 80mm finder at 12.5x using a H-beta filter.  Switching to my 18-inch at 73x (with a H-beta or UHC filter) it appeared very extended SW-NE or WSW-ENE, roughly 40'x8' and involved a mag 8 star.  The brightest portion is to the NE of the star and a number of similar magnitude stars are involved with this portion.  Removing the filter, this section was still visible though the contrast was higher using a UHC filter.  To the SW of the star, this river of nebulosity takes a mild bend and flows more towards the south.  Another fainter section of nebulosity (not included in the size estimate) spreads out to the NNW of the mag 8 star.

visualUpdates.Name: vdB 130
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (9/5/26): at 176x; this cluster mostly consists of a NW-SE string of ~8 stars. It includes a wide pair and a third star. The brightest member is mag 10.25 HD 228789.

The group is situated at the NW edge of the section of the IC 1318 complex that I've called IC 1318(f). This piece is labeled as Sh 2-108 in the Uranometria 2000.0.  The surrounding region is rich and at low power the cluster did not stand out at all, so I needed a chart to identify the stars.

visualUpdates.Name: Simeis 226
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (10/3/26): NVD at 24x; this section of the Veil lies W of the southern portion of the "Thin Thread" and E of the main southern end of NGC 6960. It appeared bright, irregular, elongated NW-SE, ~4'x3', with 3 stars involved.  Simeis 224 is 10' NW.

24" (6/26/25): NVD at 34x; section "J" is a bright, oval glow ~4' diameter. This isolated patch is situated W of the S end of the "thin thread" and 15' NW of section "I".

18" (8/3/11): this is a very dim, isolated patch of the Veil Nebula about 15' NW of section "I".  At 108x and OIII filter it appears as a very faint glow encompassing a small group of stars, ~3' diameter.  Would easily pass over this patch without noticing if not looking carefully.  Plotted on Megastar as a separate patch and on MSA as part of a western side extension at the southern end of Pickering's Wedge that includes section "I".

visualUpdates.Name: Simeis 237
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (10/3/26): NVD at 24x; Simeis 237 is a similar filament as Simeis 22, which is 12' NW. With a 6nm H-alpha filter, it was thin and very elongated N-S, ~3' in length, very good surface brightness.

24" (6/26/25): NVD at 34x; very thin short filament, isolated off the W side of the northern end of NGC 6979. Perhaps 2.5'-3' in length and oriented NNW-SSE.

18" (8/2/11): this anonymous filament in the Veil Nebula is detached off the NW end of NGC 6979 near the north-central end of the entire Cygnus loop.  At 108x and OIII filter it was easily visible as very elongated wisp oriented NNW-SSE, ~2.5'x0.5' in length.

visualUpdates.Name: Simeis 239
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (10/3/26): NVD at 24x; fairly faint but easily identified, thin filament between a mag 10.6 star at the SSE end and a mag 9.2 star just E of the north end.   The filament fades here and faintly continues to the NNW.

18" (8/27/11): easily picked up at 73x using an OIII filter as a fairly large, thin streamer oriented SSE to NNW.  The filament begins at a 10.5-magnitude star located at 20h 50m 51s +31° 27.2' and flows to the NNW.  It passes to the west of 9th magnitude SAO 70569 and fades and possibly spreads out as the thread continues to the NW.  The southern end of NGC 6974 lies in the field to the NE and the northern end of Pickering's Wisp is to the west, but this filament appears detached from both.

visualUpdates.Name: Veil Nebula (H)
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (10/3/26): NVD at 24x; bright, small, isolated patch with the H-alpha filter, about 2.5' in length. Elongated N-S and tapers on the N end, creating a small wedge.

18" (8/2/11): this is a small patch about 35' S of the feathery side branches at the southern end of NGC 6992 (the main eastern section).  It was easily swept up at 108x using an OIII filter as a fairly bright but fairly small patch, roughly triangular shaped and ~2'x1.2' diameter.  A few faint stars are superimposed including one at the SW end.  Not plotted on Megastar nor MSA but shown on the U2000 atlas.

visualUpdates.Name: Sh 2-113
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (10/6/26): NVD at 34x; Sh 2-113 is the southern end of a large, irregular ring-like nebula, extending over 45' N-S, with Sh 2-114 at the N apex. Just off the SW side of the ring is mag 5.9 HD 203156.

The brightest part of Sh 2-113 is a fairly faint, elongated patch SW-NE, 5'-6' in length. One or two stars are involved and a few more are along the eastern edge. HD 203156 is ~24' WNW.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 7209
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
8" (10/6/26): at 109x; NGC 7209 resides in an extremely rich 55' field. It is fairly rich, though not dense, and the western half partially divided by a starless lane that is oriented SE to NW.  The cluster contains many 11th mag stars and features a curving chain of stars oriented WNW to ESE.  Mag 10-10.5 SS Lac is on the SW side of the cluster, and 1.7 to its S is BRT 1157, a mag 11.1/12 pair at 7". At total of ~75 stars were counted at 229x.

14.5" (10/3/26): moderately rich cluster of 100-120 stars mag 9.5-14 at 132x in a 20' field. The most eye-catching subgroup is a striking, irregular chain with a number of 10th-11th mag stars on the N side that winds ESE to WNW. Just S of this chain are starless holes.  Additional 10th-11th mag stars are on the S side, including the 10th mag former eclipsing variable SS Lac.  The cluster calls for a low power as it is spread out and within a rich region of the Milky Way.

24" (8/12/26): very nice, low power Milky Way cluster and field. At 125x, at least 125 stars resolve, including numerous 10th and 11th mag stars with some brighter stars around the periphery. The cluster extends roughly 20', but there is no distinct boundary to measure. The most distinctive feature is a winding stream of 10th and 11th mag stars that start at the SE end, extend to the north, and then bend to the W. The stream can be broken into three distinct sections or groups at the SE side, E side and NW side ("Y" shaped in eyepiece).

15x50 IS binoculars (6/19/09): while observing Barnard 168, the fairly prominent, long dark lane that begins near M39 and heads east in the direction of the Cocoon Nebula (IC 5146), I picked up this fairly faint, round, diffuse patch that was easily visible in binoculars.  NGC 7209 is perhaps two degrees further ESE and collinear with the B168 dark lane.

17.5" (10/12/85): 100-125 stars are resolved, bright, large.  Located in a very rich field so does not stand out conspicuously. 

13.1" (9/22/84): about 75 stars, bright, fairly scattered. 

8": fairly large, spread out, similar magnitudes.  Framed by an 8th magnitude star.

visualUpdates.Name: IC 1434
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
8" (10/5/26): the main cluster includes four mag 9.5, 10, 10.5, and 11 stars on the S side and a faint NW-SE string of stars through the center.  A long chain of stars extends well beyond the cluster on the E side, angling to the ENE. A total of 30-35 stars are resolved in an 8' region at 263x.

14.5" (9/7/26): At 122x, IC 1434 is a rich cluster in a densely packed Lacerta star field!  At 158x, roughly 175 stars are resolved in a 12' region, many from mag 13-14.  The 4 brightest stars shine at mag 9.6, 9.9, 10.5, and 11.1 – all on the S side, with the latter 3 forming a triangle with sides of length 1.2' to 2.2'.

Many of the stars are arranged in 4 main long chains with offshoots that intersect N of center, where there are 3 mag 11.0-12.6 stars.  A 10' long chain heads ENE (beyond the cluster's boundary) from these stars. Another string extends 6' to the WSW (essentially continuing the first one to a total length of 16') and it includes a triple star near its WSW end. A 7' chain meanders 7' WSW from center and a 4th chain extends  4' ENE. The latter two also appear to join near the 3 brighter stars. The general region is quite rich, so the cluster is not well detached.

17.5" (7/29/92): about 100 stars in a 15' diameter.  Three mag 9 stars form a triangle on the south side.  The extensions almost fill the 20' field.  Long sprays of stars intersect near the center at a mag 10.5 star.  A long ray extends ENE for 11' and contains 30 stars.  A ray to the WSW of 11' length has 16 stars including a close triple star.  There are two more sprays to the NW of 6' length.  The cluster has no distinct borders.  The surrounding Lacerta Milky Way region is breathtaking, scanning with a 20 mm Nagler.  Located 2.1° WNW of mag 4.4 Beta Lacertae.

8" (8/12/83): ~50 stars over haze at 200x. Includes two strings on the east side, brighter stars at the south edge.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 7235
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (10/3/26): at 226x; at least two dozen stars are resolved in a 5'x3' group, extemded roughly E-W.  The brightest mag 8.7 star, which forms the NW vertex of a distinctive triangle, is somewhat isolated on the SE side. Most of the stars lie just N along a stream that extends ENE to WSW. It includes a mag 10.1 star near the ENE end (1' N of the mag 8.7 star) and a mag 10.6 star at the WSW end.

18" (8/17/04): at 225x, nearly three dozen stars are resolved in a 4'x3' group, slightly extended E-W.  The brightest mag 9 star is at the east end.  A rich stream of faint stars over haze is the north side and angling WSW towards a mag 10.5 star on the west end.

17.5" (11/2/91): two dozen stars mag 9-15 in a 4' diameter at 220x.  This moderately concentrated group is elongated WNW-ESE and includes several fairly bright stars.  A mag 9 star is at the east end and there are eight other mag 10-11 stars.  Just west of the mag 9 star is a 1.5' circular hole with no stars.  A mag 10 star at the extreme west edge has 6 faint stars mag 13/14 close following.

A compact group of faint stars 13' S appears as a small, partially resolved nebulous glow at 100x.  At 220x, 7 stars are resolved from mag 14-15.5 within a 1.5' diameter.  I had taken this as NGC 7234 but Corwin's re-reduced position from William Herschel indicates that NGC 7234 is identical to NGC 7235.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 7243
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
8" (10/6/26): at 109x, NGC 7243 is an attractive, large cluster that appears detached in the 55' eyepiece field.  Overall, it is fairly scattered (no rich subgroups) with a mostly starless region on the N side. The brighter 9th to 11th mag stars roughly form a "butterfly" outline with open wings (using some imagination). At the center is the 9" pair STF 2890, forming the vertex of a triangle with similar stars.  Increasing to 229x, a total of 80-100 stars were resolved.

14.5" (9/7/26): at 132x, NGC 7243 appeared large, fairly rich, with at least 175 stars resolved in a 21' field. The cluster mainly consists of three subgroups with a mostly star-free lane oriented SW-NE that divides the cluster. The NE subgroup includes several brighter stars mag 9.3/9.3/10.1/10.2, and 10.6. Right in the center is nice triangle (with a 4th star) and the SE vertex is STF 2890, a 9" pair of matched mag 9.4/9.7 stars.  Three brighter mag 8.5/8.7/10.5 stars are directly W.  On the S end is a larger, scattered subgroup that includes a 9th mag star and two 10th mag stars.

17.5" (10/12/85): at 83x, 150-200 stars are visible in a 20' field.  This is a striking cluster at low power and includes a number of fairly bright stars.  Near the center is the nice pair STF 2890 = 9.4/9.7 at 9".  The cluster is irregularly distributed into subgroups.

13.1" (9/22/84): about 80 stars resolved, rich, fairly large, excellent low power field, includes double star STF 2890.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 7245
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
8" (10/6/26): at 229x; a glowing knot with several very faint stars resolved sits at the center of this compact open cluster. A long chain of stars from mag 11.3-13.5 begins ~1.5' W of the knot and extends ~4.4' NW, ending outside the cluster.  A total of 15-20 stars were resolved in a 4' circle.

14.5" (10/3/26): at 226x; fairly small 4' group, rich in faint stars. Nearly three dozen stars counted at 226x. At the center, is a rich, glowing clump of stars 1' across that is partially resolved. This knot lies along the N side of a triangle containing a mag 8.8 star (off the NE end of the cluster), a mag 10.7 star (S end of cluster), and a mag 11.3 star (1.5' W of center). King 9, a smaller rich group, is just 5' NNE.

18" (8/27/05): small, rich group at 323x with at least three dozen stars resolved within the borders of an isosceles triangle (long sides ~4') formed by a mag 8.9 star (HD 235771) at the NE corner and two mag 10.7/10.9 stars on the W and S sides.  Contains a rich, 1' ball of stars that follows the brighter star on the W side.

King 9 is close NE.  At 323x, this rich, distant cluster appeared as a very small, faint knot of stars is just south of a mag 13.5-14 stars.  Perhaps a half-dozen stars were resolved, though these may be superimposed field stars as the brightest cluster members are ~16.5.

17.5" (8/5/94): about two dozen stars in a 2.5' diameter bordered by a mag 11 star on the west edge, a mag 10 star on the SSE edge and a mag 9 star (SAO 34240) off the NE side.  A small 1' diameter core is richer.  A large dust lane appears to cut through the 20' field SW-NE and passes the E side of cluster.  At low power, other dark patches are evident.  Open cluster IC 1442 is in the low power field 20' SE.

13.1" (9/9/83): about 20 fainter stars mostly in a string.  Other rich enhancements are near in this Milky Way field.  

8": 15 faint stars elongated N-S with a double star at the north edge.  Includes three brighter stars mag 8-10 around the edges but the rest of the stars are mag 13 or fainter.

visualUpdates.Name: King 9
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (10/3/26): King 9 lies only 5' NNE of NGC 7245 in a very rich Milky Way field, but it lies far in the background (~25,000 l.y.) and is 2.5-3.0 billion years old. At 226x, I noticed a faint, small elongated glow, just 1' in length N-S. Only 2 or 3 stars were resolved including the brightest mag 13.5 star at or just off the N end. The brightest member stars, though, are 17th-18th mag.

18" (8/27/05): this rich, distant cluster is close NNE of NGC 7245.  At 323x, a very small, faint knot of stars is just south of a mag 13.5-14 star.  Perhaps a half-dozen stars were resolved, though these may be superimposed field stars as the brightest cluster members are ~16.5.

visualUpdates.Name: IC 1442
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (9/7/26): at 226x, IC 1442 is an elongated, rich cluster extending SW to NE, over a glowing background of unresolved stars. Roughly 30 stars were counted in a 5' region. A fairly distinctive circlet of star (1.5' diameter) is at the NE end and a second partial ring of stars (1.5' across) is on the SW end.  A few stars seem to connect the two rings. A mag 9.2 star (HD 235778) is off the NE side and mag 8.7 HD 235777 is off the SE side.

17.5" (8/5/94): about three dozen stars in a distinctive curving row oriented SW-NE about 4' diameter with fainter loops at both ends.  A mag 9 star SAO 34248 is off the SE and a mag 10 star SAO 34250 is off the NE end.  The cluster is not concentrated, but it stands out well at low power (100x).  Located 20' SE of NGC 7245 (misplotted on MegaStar).

8" (10/5/26): at 263x; 15 stars resolved in a 5' region including a circular loop on the NE end.

C-8 (from El Cerrito): 20 stars mag 8-12 in 9' field, spread out, not rich.  Located 20' SSE of NGC 7245.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 7296
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
8" (10/5/26): 20-24 stars resolved at 263x including a single brighter mag 9.7 star at the WNW end.  Three chains of stars extend to the NE, SE, and E (the latter splits into two), creating a walking stick figure, with the brighter star representing the head.

14.5" (10/3/26): at 132x; small, elongated group of 25-30 stars, rich in faint stars. A mag 9.7 star is on the WNW end. At 226x, 30-35 stars are resolved in a 4' circle. A chain of 4 stars (each about 1' apart) extends E, then NE, from the mag 9.7 star. About 1' NE of the bright star is a small, rich clump, and another rich knot is S of center. The cluster is situated within a rich Lacerta star field, so it isn't isolated or eye-catching.

17.5" (10/5/91): compact group of roughly 30 stars in a 3'x2' area elongated N-S.  A mag 9 star is at the NW edge.  Most stars are arranged in a curved arc roughly N-S.  A string of four perfectly collinear stars trail from this arc to the NE.  Not particularly distinctive as located in a rich star field.  Contains about ten faint stars mag 14-14.5.  Located 40' E of Beta Lacertae (V = 4.4).

8" (11/8/80): 15 stars extended N-S between two mag 8.7 and 9.7 stars to the S and NNW, respectively.  Appears faint and small with an unresolved background haze.

visualUpdates.Name: Berkeley 96
visualUpdates.Visual Description: 14.5" (9/7/26): at 226x; a total of 8-10 stars were resolved in a small 2.5' circle. The main attraction is the triple star Stein 2801, which includes a mag 10.5 primary and two mag 12 companions 7" N and 10" NE.  An 11th mag star is at the SW edge and another mag 11.8 star is at the N edge.

visualUpdates.Name: Me 2-2
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (9/7/26): Me 2-2 was easy to pinpoint using mag 4.4 5 Lac, which is just 23' away. It forms a "double" with a mag 11.8 star 32" WNW. Unfiltered, the PN is comparable or slightly brighter than this star.  Excellent contrast gain blinking with a NPB filter at 158x as Me 2-2 appears up to 3 magnitudes brighter than the comparison star.  It appears very small, but non-stellar at 395x, particularly with averted vision, which causes the halo to slightly swell. The tiny disc was easier to see at 566x, but only seemed a couple of arcseconds in diameter. Situated in a rich star field.

18" (11/17/08): I starhopped over to Me 2-2 from 4.4-magnitude 5 Lacertae, located 23' WSW, and identified the planetary by blinking with an OIII filter at 175x.  Without a filter, the planetary had a slightly soft appearance and a very pale, blue color.  A good comparison star is located just 32" WNW.  Me 2-2 is slightly brighter than this star unfiltered but up to 3 magnitudes brighter using an OIII filter.  A faint star is sandwiched midway between the planetary and the star 32" WNW.  No additional details were visible at 323x - just a soft bluish star, perhaps 1.5" diameter.  Situated in a rich star field.

13.1" (9/11/85, El Cerrito): visible unfiltered at 144x as a mag 12 "star".  Excellent contrast gain with OIII filter compared to a similar star just 30" NW of Me 2-2 and the planetary is quite prominent.  Situated in a rich star field with a mag 11.5 star 1.4' SE.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 7331
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
48" (10/24/14): at 488x, the long dust lane along the west side (running N-S) was very evident as the galaxy is sharply cut off at the bright edge of a thin inner spiral arm (the arm itself was not resolved). A clearly visible outer spiral arm curves sharply counterclockwise around the south side of the halo and shoots directly north.  It continues or merges into a fairly narrow arm just west of the dust lane and extends north of the central region on the west side.

24" (7/21/12): at 322x this showpiece galaxy appeared very bright, very elongated 3:1 NNW-SSE, ~9'x3'.  Contains a very bright, elongated core that is sharply concentrated with an intense stellar nucleus.  The galaxy exhibits subtle spiral structure in the outer halo and the brighter edge of the inner western arm is sharply defined as it shoots north.  Just west of this arm the light drops off sharply due to a long dust lane and the dim glow of the outer halo is clearly visible west of the lane.  Arm structure is also evident at the north and south ends of the central region.  The four background companions to the east fit snugly in the field.

18" (8/1/08): The sharp light cut-off (dust lane) was evident, running along the west side of the galaxy, and the outer halo had subtle structure and variations in brightness that suggested spiral structure.

13.1" (many dates 7/16/82 to 7/27/84): very bright, very elongated 3:1 NNW-SSE, 9'x2.5', very bright elongated core, substellar nucleus.  The west side has a sharper edge due to dust.  Four (background) companions are close following with the brightest three NGC 7335 3.5' ENE, NGC 7337 5.2' SE, NGC 7336 5.3' NE and NGC 7340 8.1' E of center.  Stephan's Quintet lies 30' SSW.  NGC 7331 is the brightest in a small group including NGC 7320 (in Stephan's Quintet).

8" (8/28/81): very bright, large, nucleus bulge, very elongated.  Two extremely faint companions to the east are just visible.

80mm (9/29/84): faint streak at 16x in the finder.

24" (7/22/25 and 7/23/25): viewed Type Ia SN 2025rbs, discovered on July 14th (one week earlier) at 17th mag. The SN is just 12" N and 4.5" W of the nucleus.  It was immediately seen at full aperture, appearing like a second stellar nucleus (brighter than NGC 7331's, which is slightly non-stellar) and was also fairly easy with the 8" off-axis mask at 229x. The next night it appeared roughly mag 12.6-12.8V and easy using the 8" aperture. (The SN peaked at 12th mag.)

24" (8/20/25): SN 2025rbs is clearly declining in brightness and roughly a magnitiude fainter than last month.

14.5" (9/5/26, 9/7/26, 9/15/26): at 176x, I viewed the Type Ia SN 2026aaiv, which was discovered just 4 days earlier on 9/1/26. With a rapid rise in brightness, it appeared as a 14th mag star 20" E and 20" S of center, at the edge of the bright core region. It was easily seen when the seeing was sharper and appeared brighter than a mag 14.06 star 1.5' NE of center. Just two nights later, the supernova had noticeably brightened, and seemed mag 13-13.5.  On 9/15/26, the SN seemed slightly brighter than a mag 12.1 star 4.6' NW of the center of the galaxy.  So, it was probably between mag 11.8-12.0.

visualUpdates.Name: Berkeley 98
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (9/7/26): at 132x and 226x, several faint stars were resolved over a glowing background.  Includes about a dozen stars in 5' roughly circular group. Two 11th mag stars are just off the NE end.

18" (9/11/10): at 285x, I resolved roughly 15-20 faint stars (mostly mag 13.5-15) in a 4’ group. The apparent members were bracketed between two mag 10 stars at the NE end and a mag 10.5 star at the SW end.  The group is unimpressive as most of the cluster members are probably too faint to resolve.  Berkeley 98 is located 20' WSW of mag 6.4 HD 215518.

visualUpdates.Name: Sh 2-161
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (7/23/25): NVD at 34x; fairly faint but easily visible wide stream of nebulosity extending through the field from NW to SE with a length of 55'.  It passes directly through mag 6.5 HD 219634 (B0-type).  A slightly brighter circular patch of ~8' diameter is centered ~13' NW of the bright star. The nebulosity also brightens somewhat on the SE end and otherwise is a bit patchy due to dust.

NGC 7538 = Sh 2-158 is ~35' SW.  The SE end leads roughly to NGC 7635, the showpiece "Bubble Nebula", which is ~55' SE of Sh 2-161.
